source_text: Atquin cum modestia et humilitate adorantes magis commendabimus deo preces nostras ne ipsis quidem manibus sublimius elatis, sed temperate ac probe elatis, ne uultu quidem in audaciam erecto. nam et ille publicanus, qui non tantum prece, sed et uultu humiliatus atque deiectus orabat, iustificatior Pharisaeo procacissimo discessit. sonos etiam uocis subiectos esse oportet, aut quantis arteriis opus est, si pro sono audiamur? deus autem non uocis, sed cordis auditor est, sicut conspector. daemonium oraculi Pythii, et mutum, inquit, intellego et non loquentem exaudio. dei aures sonum expectant? quomodo ergo oratio Ionae de imo uentre ceti per tantae bestiae uiscera ab ipsis abyssis per tantam aequoris molem ad caelum potuit euadere? quid amplius referent isti qui clarius adorant, nisi quod proximis obstrepunt? immo prodendo petitiones suas quid minus faciunt, quam si in publico orent? •
orientation: Tertullian is giving practical rules for how Christians should pray, and has just begun discussing the modest bearing of the body.
pass_a_gloss: But rather, praying with modesty and humility, we will more commend our prayers to God, not even with our hands lifted too high, but lifted temperately and properly, not even with our face raised up into boldness. For that publican too, who was praying humbled and cast down not only in prayer but also in face, departed more justified than the most shameless Pharisee. Also the sounds of the voice ought to be subdued, or how much windpipe is needed, if we are heard for the sake of sound? But God is a hearer not of the voice but of the heart, just as he is an observer. The demon of the Pythian oracle, he says, I understand the mute and I hear the one not speaking. Do the ears of God wait for sound? How then was the prayer of Jonah able to escape to heaven from the bottom of the belly of the sea monster, through the entrails of so great a beast, from the very abysses, through so great a mass of the sea? What more will those who pray more loudly gain, except that they make a din for their neighbors? Or rather, by making their petitions public, what less do they do than if they were praying in public?

choices.why: Keeps the two nouns distinct and renders adorantes as praying, matching the treatise's focus on prayer rather than general worship.
Both adverbs describe the restrained manner of lifting hands; 'properly' captures the moral sense of probe.
Preserves the directional force of in + accusative and the negative connotation of audacia as presumption.

choices.english: departed more justified than the most shameless Pharisee
choices.why: Keeps the comparative iustificatior and the superlative procacissimo, preserving the sharp contrast Tertullian draws.
rejected: went away justified rather than the shameless Pharisee
left more righteous than the very shameless Pharisee

choices.term: sonos etiam uocis subiectos esse oportet
choices.english: also the sounds of the voice ought to be subdued
choices.why: Renders subiectos as subdued, capturing the idea of keeping the voice low and under control.
rejected: the sounds of the voice should be subject
the voice's sounds must be lowered

choices.english: they make a din for their neighbors
choices.why: Obstrepo means to make noise against or at someone; 'make a din for' preserves the dative proximis and the disruptive sense.

bible_refs.note: The publican who prayed humbled and departed more justified than the Pharisee.
Jonah's prayer from the belly of the sea monster rising to heaven.

pass_b_english: But when we pray with modesty and humility, we will commend our prayers to God all the more. We should not even lift our hands too high, but lift them temperately and properly, and we should not raise our face into boldness. For that tax collector who prayed humbled and cast down, not only in his prayer but in his face, departed more justified than the most shameless Pharisee (Luke 18:14).

The sounds of the voice also ought to be subdued. How much windpipe do we need if we are heard because of our volume? God is not a hearer of the voice but of the heart, just as he is an observer of the heart. The demon of the Pythian oracle, the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, says, "I understand the mute, and I hear the one who does not speak." Do God's ears wait for sound? How then could Jonah's prayer escape from the deepest belly of the sea monster, through the entrails of so great a beast, from the very abysses, through so great a mass of water, all the way to heaven (Jonah 2:1-2)?
What more do those who pray more loudly accomplish, except that they make a din for their neighbors? Indeed, by broadcasting their requests, what less do they do than if they were praying in public?
